 Virginia Tech

CPES, Virginia Tech

Task 4.8 High Frequency GaN Converters for
Distributed Power Systems

Dr. Fred C. Lee

 197

Project Objectives: Data center is growing at a rate of 20% annually in the past
decade. With increasing cloud computing and big data, it is expected that data center
alone will consume 10% of the total electricity by 2020. Presently, all major devices
such as multi-core processors, memories, chip sets, and hard drives, et al. are powered
from a 12 volt bus. This 12 V bus architecture was developed in the early 90’s, when
power consumption was minuscule in comparison with today’s usage. The i2R related
copper loss for 12 V bus is excessive. Recently, IBM has adopted a 360 V DC bus
and 48 VDC bus for their next generation super computers. Google has adopted 48
VDC bus for their data centers. To support these power architecture changes, it is
mandatory that the power conversion devices off the utility lines to be in a form of
distributed power on the printed circuit board in the vicinity of the core processors
and memory devices. The distributed power conversion devices have to be very
efficient and with high power density to be compatible with core processors,
memories, et al. Present power conversions devices are operating at 50-100 kHz with
a power density less than 50 W/in3. An order of magnitude power density
improvement is necessary for the wide spread use of the distributed power for all
computer servers and data centers.
 The project objectives are including dramatic increase of the power density of
front-end converter from today’s 30-50 W/in3 to 100-150 W/in3, and the front-end
power processing to be fully modularized. In this manner, a customized power system
can be synthesized by using simple modular building blocks such as multi-phase
boost power factor correction (PFCs), and high voltage DC/DC converters and
DC/DC transformers (DCXs) for input/output isolation.

Project’s Contribution to the PowerAmerica Mission: The successful
demonstration of GaN devices for the chosen applications will lead to wide spread
use of GaN converters to replace the Silicon counterparts for all forms of switch-
mode power supplies including but not limited to computer, telecommunication,
network products, data centers, PV inverters, battery chargers industrial and
consumer electronics products. This paradigm shift is accompanied with significant
improvement of efficiency, power density and cost. Furthermore, the proposed GaN
based power supply with PCB winding inductor and transformer can enable a fully
automated manufacturing to greatly reduce labor content in the assembly process,
which will give U.S. very competitive position to manufacture this high performance
power supply.

Technical Approach: In the proposed effort, we will use high voltage GaN devices
for the server power supplies to push its frequency 20 folds, from today’s 50-100 kHz
to 1-5 MHz. As a result, the power density of front-end converter can be dramatically
increased from today’s 30-50 W/in3 to 100-150 W/in3.
 A 1 kW data server power system will be demonstrated with GaN based front-end
converters including multi-phase PFCs and DCX, operating at 1-5 MHz. PFC stage
will achieve 300-500W/in3 power density and 98% efficiency; DC/DC stage will
achieve 700-1000W/in3 power density and 96% efficiency. Both PFC rectifier and
DC/DC converter will be designed with PCB integrated magnetic components.
Traditional Litz wire PFC inductor on a toroidal core is hand wound with poor

 198

tolerance. In the proposed work, we will replace it with a two-phase inverse coupled
inductors with windings integrated into a four-layer printed circuit board (PCB). In
addition, we can integrate two additional inductors into the same magnetic structure
to reduce EMI noises (a patented technology developed at CPES). For DC/DC
converter, we can replace the bulky transformer with a matrix structure of 8
transformers with PCB windings. The PCB integrated magnetic design will enable a
fully automated manufacturing.

Issues, Risks and Mitigations: None

Significant Accomplishments: The driving circuit for GaN device is evaluated in the
first. As the switching speed of GaN device is much faster than its Si counterpart, the
driver should be able to handle high dv/dt and high di/dt conditions. Through our
research, a batch of noise immunity techniques are proposed including important PCB
layout rules to avoid primary-secondary overlapping, and to minimize boot-strap
charging loop; selection of small parasitic capacitance digital isolator to achieve
PWM signal level shift; and noise filter and negative bias circuits right in front of in
driver inputs. Finally, the driving circuit is developed with high noise immunity like
dv/dt>100 V/ns and di/dt>10A/ns. At the same time, the driver has propagation delay
less than 20ns and high frequency capability up to 5MHz.
 Different available 600V-class GaN devices are collected and studied including
both E-mode GaN and D-mode GaN in cascode structure. A series of double-pulse
testing are conducted with different devices in similar test setup. The measured
switching loss indicates that for all of GaN devices, the turn on loss is high and the
turn on loss is small. Furthermore, the turn off loss of E-mode GaN device is smaller
at low turn-off current and then it goes up quickly due to miller effect. On the
contrary, the cascode GaN has relatively flat turn-off loss when turn-off current
increased. This is due to the current source turn-off mechanism discovered by us.
With this deep understand of different GaN devices, we chose best candidates for
both PFC and LLC design.
 Then hard switching and soft switching is compared. Very different with many
people’s first impression, soft switching not becoming less important but becoming
even more important for GaN device to operate at MHz high frequency. This is
because hard switching brings lots of troubles to GaN device like significant turn-on
loss, poor efficiency, and tremendous parasitic ringing and related driving issues and
EMI noise issues. Soft switching is proved to be the right way to fully utilize the
advantages of GaN device particularly for MHz converter design. This conclusion is
reinforced by analysis, simulation, and experiments.
 The topology of both AC/DC stage and DC/DC stages are selected. Totem-pole
topology is becoming the most suitable one for GaN due to its simplicity and
symmetry. LLC is still considered as the most attractive topology for DC/DC stages
with higher potential offered by GaN. The totem-pole PFC can operate at 1MHz to
5MHz with >98% efficiency. The LLC converter can operate at 1MHz with >97%
efficiency.

 199

 Then packaging is becoming another bottleneck for GaN device. Traditional
packaging has large parasitics thus it limits the performance of GaN device. Packing
impact is previously studied in CPES. As a continued efforts, a preliminary module is
designed with interconnect parasitics less than 3 nH and good thermal dissipation
capability. The developed full-bridge GaN can be used for 1.2kW totem-pole PFC very
efficiently and its volume is less than 20cm3.
 Finally, magnetic design is also studied in this year. Different high frequency core
materials are evaluated by CPES proposed test setup. The core loss of each material is
measured under non-sinusoid excitation with DC bias for frequency range 1-5MHz. Then
best magnetic material for PFC inductor and DC/DC transformer are identified at 1 MHz
with core losses fully characterized according to the way they are used in the proposed
circuit operation. Specific data are including core loss density <60kW/m 3 with
Bac_pp=15mT, Fs=3MHz.

Technology to Market: The demands for AC/DC front-end converters are growing
rapidly in recent years, including but not limited to computers, telecommunication, data
centers, battery chargers, industrials, and aerospace applications. Collectively, these
products consume more than 10% of the total electric power. One percent efficiency
improvement in this industry sector represents 20 TWH of energy saving, which is
equivalent to the total energy outputs of three average size nuclear power plants, each at 7
TWH annual production. Moreover, with the increasing of cloud computing and big data,
it is expected that data center alone will consume 10% of the total electricity by 2020.
Typical 1kW AC/DC power supplies is labor intensive in terms of manufacturing and
assembling processes. Forty percent of the components are manually inserted. Thus,
manufacturing of switching power supplies are largely moved off shores to low labor cost
countries. The trend will not reverse unless there is a paradigm shift in the way we design
and manufacture these power supplies.
 Within the above mentioned industry sector, data center server power supplies are
the most performance driven, energy and cost conscious. Within a data center, all major
devices are powered from a 12V bus. This 12V bus architecture was developed in the
early 90’s, when the power consumption was minuscule in comparison with today’s
usage at 100A-200A levels per CPU. The i2R related copper loss for 12V bus is
excessive. In order to place the high voltage DC/DC converter on the CPU board (mother
board), this converter has to be very efficient and high-density to be compatible with core
processors, memories, et al. Today, power converters are designed to operate at 50-100
kHz with a power density less than 50 W/in3 and they are not suited for the intended
applications. Recently, the International Electronics Manufacturing Initiative (iNEMI) at
the behest of IBM and other server manufacturers undertook a project to develop an
industry standard for DC-DC converters. This converter is used to step down 380V
directly to 12V and placed directly on the motherboard. This architecture will eliminate
the use of bulky cables and the losses associated with them. This proposed power
architecture is deemed superior to current practice. With the elimination of online UPS
and cables and harness, the efficiency improvement is estimated at least 5%. A survey by
iNEMI suggested that the power supply with the target efficiency (97%) and form factor
(500W/in3 power density) is not readily available. It is highly unlikely to achieve this tall
order with current design practice using silicon devices. This iNEMI initiative indeed

 200

signifies a potential paradigm change and, thus, presenting a great opportunity for GaN to
make an en route to this high volume market. CPES currently has more than 80 industry
members. Many of them have direct interest in the data center related business. In this
project we will work closely with our industry members, such as Emerson, Delta
Electronics, Texas Instruments, Intel, Eaton, ABB to pursue product development for
commercialization. Since the proposed power supply is built with PCB winding inductor
and transformer, it is well suited for manufacture automation.

Plans for Next Budget Period If Funded: Building upon the advances we have made
during the Year 1 effort, the proposed work in Year 2 will be focused on developing a
MHz GaN based front-end converter with 99% efficiency for PFC stage and 97-98%
efficiency for DC/DC stage. Both PFC and DC/DC stage will achieve 700-1000W/in3
power density. This high density high efficiency front-end converter can be used in
today’s AC datacenter, as well as the next generation of Data center proposed in the
iNEMI initiative.
 There are four major goals/milestones we will achieve for next budget period. The
first one is to design coupled inductor for the dual-phase interleaved totem-pole PFC. The
coupled inductor will be integrated with PCB so it could be automatic manufactured.
Balance technique will also be applied in the coupled inductor design so that the
common-mode noise of PFC can also be reduced and the input EMI filter can be further
simplified.
 The second goal is to further optimize the DC/DC stage to meet both efficiency
and density requirement of iNEMI initiative for future Data center. This high density
DC/DC stage could be used for both AC and DC Data center
 The third goal is to optimize the design of EMI filter for the whole system. The
PFC and LLC converters will operate in series and the total EMI noise will be minimized
by applying both balancing and shielding technics. Then EMI filter for this front-end
converter will be optimized to suppress the remaining noise. It is estimated that the
structure of EMI filter can be simplified from two stage to single stage due to the MHz
high frequency operation.
 The fourth goal is to achieve programmable outputs (12V, 5V) for DC/DC stage.
This function can be realized within a single converter topology and a single digital
controller. This simple controller incorporates the CPES patented state-trajectory control
techniques with significantly improved performances including: soft start-up and short-
circuit protection to minimize stresses; auto-tuning; fast load transient response; burst
mode for light load efficiency improvement.

 Virginia Tech

CPES, Virginia Tech

4.7 High-density high-efficiency adapter

Dr. Fred C. Lee

 203

Project Objectives: One of the biggest market of power supplies, in both volume and
dollar, is the ac-dc adapter/charger for consumer electronics. Todays, most of the
adapters are operating at relative low frequency (<100 kHz) with the state-of-the-art
efficiency up to 91.5%. The adapter power density is rather meager, at 6-9 W/in3.
 The emerging gallium-nitride (GaN) device is deemed as a game changing device
in this particular application with improved efficiency and significant size reduction. Our
initial experiments using the first generation of GaN devices were conducted with 10X
increase in switching frequencies and 5X improvement in power density. We will
develop 65W and 45W adapter prototypes with GaN devices to achieve 26W/in3 and
20W/in3 in power density, respectively. The prototype efficiency should be higher than
92% and the temperature should be lower than 70℃.

Project’s Contribution to the PowerAmerica Mission: In this project, we will
collaborate with an Institute industry member to develop a GaN device with targeted
design for this application. We also partner with another Institute industry member to
develop a high-density high-efficiency adapter suitable for commercialization. More
importantly, the proposed adapter is built with PCB winding transformer, the
automation manufacture can be realized to significantly reduce labor content, which
will give U.S. very competitive position to manufacture this high performance
adapter.

Technical Approach: High frequency is the major catalyst for size reduction in the
advancement of adapter technology. The emerging GaN device, with much improved
figures of merit, opens the door for operating frequency well into the MHz range. To
realize the benefits of GaN devices resulting from significantly higher operating
frequencies, a number of issues have to be addressed, such as converter topology,
magnetics, control, packaging, gate drive and thermal management. The research team at
CPES has successfully demonstrated in the Year 1 of the program that the GaN based
adapter design is capable of operating at 1-2 MHz frequency with an improved efficiency
up to 93.5%, together with 27W/in3 density which is 3X improvement compared to the
state-of-the-art product. Since the prototype is selected at 45W and 65W power level and
hence, no power factor requirement, a simple flyback converter is chosen as shown in Fig
1. This topology is universally selected by all products under 75W for low cost.

 (a) Active clamp flyback diagram (b) preliminary prototype
 Fig. 1 MHz active clamp flyback front-end converter

Even though the topology is common, we have implemented a number of unique features

 204

as listed below:
 • Active clamp circuit is applied to recycle the transformer leakage energy and realize
 soft-switching for the primary switches. The di/dt and dv/dt are significantly
 reduced with soft-switching which is beneficial for high frequency EMI reduction.
 • Over 90% of switching related losses are eliminated by soft switching for both the
 primary side and secondary side devices, which allows for MHz or even higher
 frequency operation.
 • Common-mode noise is significantly reduced using the patented shield layer based
 on PCB winding based transformer [10]. The shielding is effective through all the
 conducted EMI testing frequency range (150kHz~30MHz) with over 20dB
 reduction of CM noises and, thus, simplifying the EMI filter design to a single-
 stage. It should be noted that the high frequency flyback transformer winding is
 implemented for the first time using only 6-layer PCB board.
 • PCB winding transformer is used to build the proposed high density adapter,
 the automation manufacture can be realized to significantly reduce labor
 content

Issues, Risks and Mitigations: None

Significant Accomplishments: During year 1 program, we have completed all the
subtasks and meet the milestones. To sum the major task of year 1:
 • We have done evaluation and characterization for different type of GaN devices,
 including enhancement mode GaN and depletion-mode GaN in cascode
 configuration. We identify that hard-switching turn-on is detrimental from both
 efficiency and noise point of view. Soft-switching is still desired for GaN at high
 frequency operation. Packaging is also critical to GaN devices in terms of switching
 loss and gate ringing. We have proposed a better package for cascode GaN devices
 which enhance the device performance significantly. Actually our package concept
 has been adopted in several manufactory’s recent GaN devices.
 • We have developed a suitable driving circuit for GaN devices, especially for high
 side switches, that can achieve high dv/dt immunity up to 150V/ns as well as fast
 driving capability.
 • We have developed a high frequency synchronous rectifier driving method to tackle
 the current oscillation which only occurred at very high frequency.
 • We have identified a suitable topology for low power adapters using active clamp
 flyback converter. This topology can recycle the transformer leakage energy and
 realize ZVS for primary switches which is beneficial for both efficiency and EMI
 aspect.
 • We have applied shielding technique to reduce the common-mode noise which can
 further increase the corner frequency of the EMI filter, and therefore, shrink the
 filter size significantly.
 • We have used finite-element-analysis to model and design the preliminary PCB
 winding based transformer to achieve small winding loss and leakage inductance.
 It should be noted that the high frequency flyback transformer winding is
 implemented for the first time using only 6-layer PCB board including shielding

 205

 layer.
 • We have designed a preliminary power-stage hardware to demonstrate the
 advantage and benefits of increasing the switching frequency with GaN devices.
 We have achieved above 93% in efficiency and over 27W/in3 in power density.

Technology to Market: One of the biggest market of power supplies, in both volume
and dollar, is the ac-dc adapter/charger for consumer electronics, including laptop, tablet,
smart phone, mobile devices, game console, printer, and stereo sound-bars, etc. The
market is projected to surpass $8 billion in 2015 and reach $9 billion by 2018; with much
of this growth being driven by smart phones, tablets and a number of emerging
applications. CPES currently has more than 80 industry members. Many of them have
potential to commercialize the proposed high frequency GaN adapter. In this project we
will work closely with our industry members, such as Texas Instruments, ON
Semiconductor, Sonos, Delta Electronics, to pursue product development for
commercialization.
Plans for Next Budget Period If Funded: We want to improve the year 1 design with
higher efficiency and density as well as standardized system structure for wide power
range adapters. As the plan of year 2 program, we will work on an innovative universal
topology that is based on a two-stage approach as show in Fig.2. For power less than
75W, the first stage serves two functions: 1) to replace the diode bridge with active
switches. The expect efficiency improvement is about 0.5-1%; 2) Instead of serving as a
PFC circuit, the first stage can provide harmonic injection, resulting to a much reduced
bulk capacitor. For power greater than 75W, the first stage will serve as a bridgeless PFC.
This topology, while not practical for silicon devices due to excessive switching losses
and body diode losses, is deemed very effective for GaN devices operating in multi-
megahertz. The bulky electrical capacitor can also be reduced to some extend with
harmonic injection as long as the input current can meet the requirement (IEC 61000-3-
2). The second stage is a LLC resonant converter and is usually operating at a semi-
regulated mode. The switching frequency is very close to resonant frequency to minimize
conduction loss and switching loss. The SR driving signal can be the same as the primary
PWM signal that can significantly simplify the system control. The transformer of the
2nd stage will be implemented using PCB winding for efficiency, density and easy
automation consideration. The anticipated system efficiency is over 95% and the power
density can reach 50W/in3.

X-FAB Texas, Inc.

Task 2.1: SiC Power Device Commercial Foundry
Development

Andy Wilson, andy.wilson@xfab.com

 208

Project Objectives: X-FAB Texas will develop a “device agnostic” 6-inch silicon
carbide (SiC) commercial foundry. Ultimately, the transition to a commercial foundry
model for SiC power device fabrication will enable companies with a variety of device
technologies (Diodes, JFETs, MOSFETs, etc.) to utilize the foundry for volume
production. Rather than building a SiC fab from scratch, an existing 6-inch silicon
foundry will be converted to process SiC wafers. This approach will leverage existing
silicon processing equipment, but will require the addition of specialized equipment
unique to SiC processing as well as the development of SiC unit processes that can be run
on the existing silicon processing equipment.
 To provide scalability such that multiple companies can use the foundry for their
device of interest a Process Installation Kit model will be used. In addition to having a
baseline process in place, this will allow companies to transfer their existing process
flows to the 6-inch SiC wafer foundry while maintaining propriety control over specific
process steps that may be viewed as critical IP. By sharing baseline unit process steps
and the capacity that will be installed, Institute member companies will enjoy the cost
and scalability benefits of a large wafer fabrication facility even though they would not
individually be in a position to support such a large scale operation. By establishing this
foundry domestically, Institute members will not need to send their production overseas
which could jeopardize the security of their design and process IP.

Project’s Contribution to the PowerAmerica Mission: The Open SiC Device foundry
established in this task will be instrumental in achieving the DOE’s goal of price parity
between SiC and Si devices. Bringing the scale and manufacturing efficiency of an
established Silicon foundry to Silicon Carbide will enable drastic reductions in the cost to
process a 6-inch SiC wafer. Additionally, a foundry will be able to aggregate the SiC
EpiWafer demand of multiple customers and bring the purchasing power to the market
that will reduce the cost of SiC starting wafers. Finally X-FAB will work to establish
Standard process (Subtask 2.1.5) that will enable process harmonization and cost
reductions for all customers utilizing the Open Foundry.

Technical Approach: Over 90% of the processes required to fabricate a Silicon Carbide
device wafer can be realized on standard silicon fabrication equipment. This equipment
will need to be modified in order to accommodate the fact that SiC wafers are thinner
than Si wafers and transparent while Si wafers are opaque. The tool modifications
performed as part of Subtask 2.1.3 will result in existing Silicon tools installed in X-FAB
Texas being able to run both Silicon and Silicon Carbide wafers. This model will allow
the fixed costs related to these tools to be shared between both Silicon and SiC
production enabling a more cost effective approach than a model where a dedicated SiC
line is established and SiC wafers must absorb the full fixed cost.
 For the processes that cannot be supported on existing tools, equipment will be
purchased as part of Subtask 2.1.1 to develop a pilot line within the X-FAB Silicon
foundry fab that will close these gaps and provide capability to support all processes that
are required to fabricate SiC Device Wafers.

Issues, Risks and Mitigations: It should be recognized that establishing a full flow SiC
open foundry line in parallel with a running Silicon foundry fab has never been

 209

demonstrated. Risks exist with regards to cross-contamination of non-compatible
materials, inability of Silicon based tools to achieve required capability in SiC processes
as well as demonstration of the concept to run Si and SiC interchangeably on shared
equipment. Risk will be mitigated by providing for equipment redundancy (when
possible), along with establishing and maintaining relationships with external processing
vendors that would allow for continuation of support in the event that internal capabilities
are compromised.

Significant Accomplishments: The X-FAB Texas team has accomplished most of the
milestones ahead of schedule. Working with Institute device partners, the team has been
successful in establishing the wafer processing capabilities defined in Task 2.1 and have
delivered 6-inch SiC wafers to device partners that contain functional devices.
Outsourced processes have been brought in-house as equipment is installed and qualified
providing the foundation for cost and cycle time improvements.

Technology to Market: As a make function, X-FAB’s contributions to Technology to
Market center around the ability to enable our device customers to quickly bring their
products to market, reduce their costs and continue to innovate with both process and
design optimizations.

Plans for Next Budget Period If Funded: X-FAB plans to purchase and install a high
temperature Al implanter in BP2. With this final piece of equipment, the X-FAB Texas
SiC pilot production line will have capability to fully process SiC Power Device wafers
without relying on outsourced steps. Eliminating reliance on outsourcing is critical to
meeting the pricing targets established by the PowerAmerica. X-FAB also plans to add
inspection tools in BP2. Given the high cost of starting SiC Epiwafers, the cost of scrap
is more significant than with Silicon. To reach the PowerAmerica pricing targets, the
following inspection tools will be required to support Yield Enhancement and process
control improvement activities.
 • Patterned Wafer Defect Inspection Tool
 • Un-patterned Film Defect Inspection Tool
 • Film Thickness Ellipsometer

X- FAB also plans the continued development of Generic Unit Processes that has been
started in Budget Period 1. The proposed generic unit processes for development in BP2
are:
 • Self-Aligned Channel Implant Mask (2-Stage)
 • Diode ILD (SiN and/or SiO2)
 • Backside Ohmic Metal and Laser Anneal
 • Schottky Contact (Surface preparation, metal deposition and anneal)
 • Polysilicon Gate Formation
 • Backside Metal Stack

Project Output: The primary output of Task 2.1 is to establish the manufacturing
capability and cost structure that will enable the success of SiC device partners and

 210

accelerate the adoption of WBG devices in the market. We have however delivered
several technical reports to PowerAmerica as output of Task 2.1:

 • High temperature implant ROI analysis report evaluating high temperature
 implant options for foundry operations
 • Process Installation Kit Specifications
 o Generic Unit Process Specification – Polyimide Protective Overcoat
 o Generic Unit Process Specification – Frontside Power Metal (4um)
 o Generic Unit Process Specification – Frontside Power Metal (5um)
 o Generic Unit Process Specification – SiC MOSFET ILD Layer
 o Generic Unit Process Specification – Implant Blocking Oxide Hard Mask

BP2 SYNOPSIS
The Institute and all its programs and activities were fully up and running
in BP2. Membership continued to grow as the Institute established itself
throughout the industry as the premier clearinghouse for information
and technology related to WBG semiconductor power electronics. The
Annual Meeting, WBG Summer Workshop, the fall Short Course, and
having a presence at large industry conferences helped to cement that
reputation. The Membership Advisory Committee continued to represent
the voice of industry and make recommendations for future technical
direction. The Membership Initiated Projects and Open Innovation fund
activities were established.

A new slate of projects in Focus Areas 2 through 5, selected through the
competitive annual project call, were initiated. Considerable resources
were focused on continuing to support the enhancement of capabilities
at X-FAB to produce SiC semiconductors at scale. The device bank
was established and stocked with project deliverables and purchased
semiconductor devices. This resource was conceived to quickly provide
engineering samples to researchers in order to avoid project delays
caused by long lead time items.

Dr. Victor Veliadis was hired as the Chief Technology Officer, and he
would eventually take over the position of Executive Director as well.

 214

Creating a Roadmap for SiC and GaN
Collaboration is a key driving force of PowerAmerica, and the institute’s
technological roadmap is the best example of this principle in action. The roadmap
was developed by PowerAmerica members working closely to condense their
extensive knowledge of technical, market and supply chain objectives into a
cohesive plan to guide the institute’s technical activities in the coming years.
Wide bandgap technologies have the potential to reduce energy consumption and
harmful emissions in a variety of industries, while also creating manufacturing
jobs across the United States. To capitalize on this potential, the roadmap
offers a strategy for making WBG semiconductors
cost competitive with silicon-based power electronics
and accelerating the adoption of SiC- and GaN-based
components in new markets and applications.

The Process
To create the roadmap, the institute’s semiconductor
and power electronics experts met first in person,
then virtually over several months, to discuss technical
challenges, determine research priorities and come to
an agreement on current status and near and long term
targets for development. While challenging, this process
helped cement strong working relationships between
members and created a process for future roadmap
updates, which will occur annually.

Key Roadmap Features:
• Identifies the key markets and application areas
  for SiC and GaN power electronics;
• Estimates the timeframe when they will be A public version of the
  commercially viable; roadmap is available on the
• Estimates the performance targets GaN and SiC PowerAmerica website, while
  technologies are expected to meet over time; a more detailed version is
 available to members only.
• Identifies the technical barriers to achieving
  those targets; and
• Identifies the activities needed to overcome
  those barriers.

The roadmap will guide PowerAmerica’s strategic
decisions for demonstrating the benefits of SiC and
GaN, improving wide bandgap semiconductor device
performance, and increasing commercial use of
these technologies.

Module Development and Manufacturing 2017

Terrestrial Neutron Induced Reliability Concerns in Very High Voltage
Silicon Carbide Power Devices

Terrestrial neutrons are byproducts of cosmic ray
interactions with the earth’s atmosphere. Due to their
charge neutrality, these neutrons are capable of traveling
vast distances in the atmosphere, even reaching sea
level with relative abundance. These neutrons have been
shown to cause failures in power devices via interactions
with lattice atoms. These neutron induced single event
effects are not new and were first reported in the late
1990s in Si power devices. Unlike Silicon, reliability
of SiC devices is a big unknown for power and energy
system designers since they lack legacy data due to their
recent adoption. The absence of data for this type of
long-term reliability problem has been an obstacle for the
accelerated adoption of SiC. These measurements and
data mitigate this perceived “prejudice” by presenting the
empirical results and also comparisons to similarly rated
silicon parts. CoolCAD Electronics,
 Left: Terrestrial neutron induced SiC power device failures.
 Right: Terrestrial neutron cosmic shower. LLC

 254

BP3 SYNOPSIS
BP3 saw the Insttitute mature and grow its reach. Membership grew
steadily and the number of projects also increased. More projects
were awarded in Focus Area four to demonstrate the cost, size, weight,
and efficiency advantages of WBG technology in renewable energy,
data center, electric transport,consumer electronics, and other energy
applications. The first Member Initiated Project was awarded in this
budget period. The MIPs are a tool that allows members to use their
pooled dues to define and award a precompetitive project that meets a
specific need or fills a knowledge gap. The MIP project results and any
resulting IP are shared among the members. The technology roadmap
was also significantly revised with guidance from industry. The roadmap
identifies the timelines for technology maturation, sets technical targets
for semiconductor device performance, and identifies knowledge gaps
that are candidates for future MIP topics that the Institute could address.

BP4 SYNOPSIS
Member engagement increased as evidenced by the establishment
of working groups to review the bylaws for post-DoE changes, review
MIP proposals, and select another round of MIP projects for award.
PowerAmerica has been fortunate that the Membership Advisory
Committee chair and vice chair have always been high level industry
experts with broad experience and deep insights. They have given
generously of their time and made valuable contributions to the planning
for sustainability. During BP4, the MAC developed its first Operating
Plan for sustainability. This document described the plans for the
Institute after DoE funding ends in BP5. It described the structure of
the organization, the estimated budget, long term objectives, and other
parameters. It was also acknowledged that the ByLaws would need to
be revisited for the post-DoE period.

BP5 SYNOPSIS
This last round of cost shared projects was awarded from the annual
project call. In addition, four new Member Initiated Projects MIPs (funded
exclusively with member dues) were awarded as well. The leadership
and staff began the process of planning for the eventual closeout of all
the DoE supported tasks at the end of BP5. At the direction of the MAC,
a new scholarship program was started that awarded a small stipend to
university students working on WBG technology. Students receiving the
scholarship will be invited to present their work at the Annual Meeting
each year.

 A record of
 accomplishment
 As we conclude our fifth year as a Department of Energy-
 backed, Manufacturing USA institute, PowerAmerica takes great
 pride in our institute’s accomplishments to date. Together with
 our members, we’ve built a strong network of technologists
 and manufacturers—moving wide bandgap semiconductor
 technology out of the lab and onto the assembly line. Member
 projects have created jobs and spurred innovation that has
 resulted in more powerful, more efficient devices across a range
 of applications. We look forward to continuing our mission as a
 self-sufficient, member-driven organization.

PowerAmerica funded Applications

 2015-2020 Harnessing the capabilities of wide bandgap semiconductors
 can lead to dramatic energy savings in industrial processes,
 data centers, and consumer devices; increase electric vehicle
73 industry driving range; and help integrate renewable energy onto the
 electric grid.

Power in membership
PowerAmerica provides a forum for members to improve the
performance of SiC and GaN power semiconductor technology
and develop new, clean energy applications. Our membership
network spans the wide bandgap technology ecosystem, from
materials to device developers and foundries to module
manufacturers to end users, as well as universities that
educate and supply the future workforce. As we continue to
grow, so does the diversity of our membership.

BP6 SYNOPSIS
Through discussions with DoE, it was decided to award a two year
BP6 (May 2021 through April 2023) for the purpose of spending the
approximately $5M in program income that has accumulated since
the inception of the program. This was later extended to August 2023
to allow the final round of MIPs to run to completion. Throughout BP6,
only MIP projects were carried out, demonstrating the PowerAmerica
had achieved sustainability and stability. Three successive rounds
of MIP projects were awarded during this time, al driven by member
recommendations and priorities. Unfortunately during this time, most
explicit EWD activities (Focus Area 5) were shelved. However, most
MIPs were actually led by university members and everyone had at least
one university as a member of a team, working with an industry member.
The slate of MIPs increased during BP6 and the majority of those funds
will be directed at these important projects.

The Institute reduced its staffing levels, reduced the size of its HQ office
space, and made other cost reduction changes in order to reduce its
operating costs and streamline operations. Even with those changes, the
institute continues to provide service to our members and an attractive
value proposition.

 375

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The US Department of Energy’s Advanced Manufacturing Office (predecessor to
AMMTO) established PowerAmerica in December 2014 for the purpose of developing
and accelerating the adoption of wide bandgap (WBG) semiconductor technology. The
objective was to spark early commercialization of energy efficient products, educate
a trained workforce, create high tech jobs, and nurture the growth of the US WBG
semiconductor manufacturing industry. PowerAmerica is led by North Carolina State
University by way of a five year, $140M cooperative agreement with DoE. This private-
public partnership with DoE includes member companies ranging from startups, small-
medium enterprises, to large system integrators, world-class universities, and several
national labs. The wide bandgap power electronic ecosystem formed by these
diverse Institute members is focused on using advanced manufacturing to 1) lower the
cost of silicon carbide and gallium nitride semiconductor devices to be comparable to
silicon devices, 2) demonstrate the size, weight, and energy efficiency advantages of
WBG semiconductor power electronics through system demonstrations that validate
their effectiveness, and 3) building an education pipeline for a skilled workforce to
meet the future demand for emerging WBG semiconductor markets to enhance US
economic competitiveness globally.

By the end of Budget Period 6 (August 2023), PowerAmerica had achieved most of its
major objectives in technology development, semiconductor device cost reduction,
ecosystem growth & engagement, and education & workforce development. Through
strategic foundry investments, we helped to establish the first US SiC foundry (X-FAB)
and supported a second (Microchip) to move closer to volume production. We have
successfully demonstrated the energy and system benefits of WBG technology
through demonstration projects with some of the biggest US manufacturers of
energy intensive equipment (John Deere, GE, United Technologies, Raytheon, United
Technologies, and others). We have brought the unique capabilities and facilities
of the national labs to help solve challenging technical problems for industry (Naval
Research Laboratory, National Renewable Energy Laboratory). The PowerAmerica
name has become synonymous with WBG technology advancement from our many
webinars, tutorials, annual events, and presence at major energy and electronics
conferences around the world. We have helped bring together companies from
different parts of the supply chain, resulting in several successful new partnerships
and business relationships. The commercial interest in WBG technology is higher than
ever and companies and governments around the world have announced hundreds
of millions of dollars in future investment to build capacity and compete with silicon
in new markets and applications. We have trained hundreds of engineering students
from universities across the US through hands-on projects and coursework. Working
professionals have also benefited from our many targeted short courses and tutorials
through the years. In short, PowerAmerica has made great strides in each of our key
objectives and the organization currently operates without government support. The
organization is member driven, member supported, and is laser focused on the needs
and priorities of the industry.
 376

CREATING A VIBRANT &
ENGAGED WBG ECOSYSTEM
PowerAmerica has had a positive, measurable impact on power semiconductor development and
manufacturing in the US. From 2015 to the present, the technology has matured considerably,
commercial applications have grown, sales volumes of SiC and GaN have multiplied, and
companies across the supply chain have grown and prospered. We have brought together many
of the leading companies, academic researchers, as well as National Lab and other stakeholders
to address key challenges and forge partnerships. PowerAmerica members regularly comment
that one of the primary benefits they derive from membership is the networking and information
exchange that takes place at our semi-annual events. Because our membership has grown in
recent years has been primarily from companies within the semiconductor supply chain rather
than end users. This points to the dynamic nature of the industry as customers, competitors, and
new entrants to the market want a seat at the table.

We’ve strived to be member-driven and member-focused from the start; and that has contributed
to our success. Our members in turn have invested considerable time in guiding our technology
roadmap, spreading the word about PowerAmerica, contributing to education efforts, and
helping us understand their challenges. Several new companies have come to us asking to join
because a current member company told them about PowerAmerica and what we do. The
Member Advisory Committee (MAC) is the voice of the industry and the forum for important
discussions about governance, financial planning, and technical direction. One example of this
process is the portfolio of 26 Member Initiated Projects (MIP) over the past four years that are
funded solely with member dues and focused on member technical challenges. From selecting
the technical topics to reviewing proposals and reviewing the project’s results, the MIPs
represent the voice of industry in guiding research that addresses crosscutting challenges to
wider WBG adoption. MIPs also typically involve a university teamed with a company or National
Lab, helping to ensure that the task is appropriately focused and that results and know-how are
shared appropriately. Members have also contributed valuable time to our education efforts
such as the annual WBG Short Course, bi-annual tutorials, technical webinars, special panels at
large semiconder industry conferences, and supporting our undergraduate student scholarships.
Member dues have also sustained PowerAmerica after DoiE funding indeed in April 2021.
Membership has grown steadily and now stands at 90. Importantly, the growth has been mainly
in companies in the core device fabrication and power electronic integration sectors of the
market. Most new members
are customers or suppliers of
existing members.

EDUCATION & WORKFORCE

The Education and Workforce Development (EWD) activities have perhaps had the
broadest reach and lasting impact of all the PowerAmerica endeavors. As the table
below indicates, hundreds of students and thousands of working professionals have
benefited from the numerous technical webinars, conference tutorials, WBG Short
Courses, and other EWD programming. In the early budget periods, EWD activities
included STEM activities for K-12 and also community college instructors. The
youth activities included campus visits to compete in model EV cars the students
built, classroom table top science kit with lessons, and activities for middle school
teachers. Community college instructors were given hands on lab activities and
instruction on electric energy principles. Since BP3, all activities have focused
on university level students and working professionals, as these two groups
represent a more targeted use of resources and better meet industry near term
needs. The undergraduate and graduate student training has been particularly
impactful because it involved a combination of classroom instruction, hands-on
technical projects, working with industry; often leading to journal publications
and conference presentations. Many former PowerAmerica students are now
employed by companies such as Wolfspeed, ABB, XFAB, Ford, and others. At the
end of BP5, there were 16 university members, each contributing in their respective
areas of expertise. By the end of BP6, university membership reached 23. University
faculty have also been funded to develop teaching modules and training tools and to
acquire specialized lab equipment that introduce WBG concepts and facilitate their
use in working circuits and systems. A searchable database on our website lists
student profiles summarizing their research experience, skills, and career interests.
The student profiles are a valuable tool for members seeking talent for internships
or employees. Member meetings have included activities such as student speed
dating with industry, poster sessions, informal networking opportunities, resume
coaching, student project presentations, and other enrichment exercises.

WBG training for working professionals is incredibly important to increasing
their use . It supports and encourages those practitioners who are experienced
working with Si semiconductors, to learn about the distinct qualities and superior
system benefits of SiC and GaN . Obtaining the best performance from SiC and
GaN requires particular design and packaging considerations and we’ve strived to
convey those in several ways. These include the annual WBG Short Course, twice
yearly tutorials concurrent with our meetings, special sessions we’ve organized at
large industry conferences (APEC, ECCE, ISCRM, WiPDA, PEDG, others), and invited
talks at member facilities to train their staff.

The table below summarizes some of the major metrics of the PowerAmerica
education and workforce education program.

 Budget Period 6
 STATEMENT OF PROJECT OBJECTIVES

 PowerAmerica: The Next Generation Power Electronics Manufacturing Innovation Institute

 A. PROJECT OBJECTIVES

The objective of this project is to effectively manage and assess the performance of PowerAmerica: a
Manufacturing USA Institute (referred to interchangeably as “PowerAmerica” or “Institute.”)

The PowerAmerica Institute is a consortium established under a Cooperative Agreement with the
Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) and led by
North Carolina State University (the prime recipient), with participation from sub- recipients of the
award, Member Companies, universities and other educational institutions, as well as other state and
federal government agencies and research organizations. DOE’s overarching role is to create the
Institute and provide oversight and stewardship of Federal funds. Further, in accordance the Terms and
Conditions, DOE will have substantial involvement in the Institute during the term of the DOE
Cooperative Agreement.

The Institute, driven by the member advisory committee (MAC), will continue to manage a Program led
by North Carolina State University (NCSU) via the Cooperative Agreement with DOE to enable
advancement of the next generation of energy-efficient, high performance power electronic devices.
With substantial guidance from its industry and academic members, the Institute leadership will
implement and execute an industry-wide technology, workforce development and infrastructure agenda
that strongly leverages industry consortia, regional clusters, and other resources in science, technology,
and economic development to accelerate and scale-up manufacturing innovation and production of wide
bandgap semiconductor (WBG) power electronics.

The Institute will manage an organizational team and leadership structure in coordination with the MAC
that:
 • Develops, implements, and tracks performance metrics, utilizes quantitative management
 tools, and employs industry best practices.
 • Meets or exceeds the Program’s technical and economic goals and objectives
 • Develops tools and methodologies to enable effective and efficient communication,
 technology transfer, and commercialization by industry.
 • Establishes and implements By-laws, Membership Agreements, policies, procedures, and all
 relevant organizational documents for effective operations.
 • Conducts business in an ethical and responsible manner.

The principal goals of PowerAmerica to achieve significant economic growth in wide bandgap power
electronics through technical leadership by reducing the cost of US based manufacturing. This will
increase the number of domestic jobs created, and provide benefits from the increased energy
productivity obtained from the system-level advantages of WBG semiconductors (i.e., size, weight,
power density, and efficiency improvements) in power electronics systems.

 736

 BP6
To meet these goals the objectives of the Institute at the end of BP5 are to:

 1. Form a self-sustaining 1, Institute composed of industry, academic and government stakeholders
 to promote the adoption and manufacturing of WBG semiconductors in power electronics.

 2. Reduce the cost and scale-up the production of WBG semiconductor power devices and modules
 through innovative foundry models and innovations in manufacturing that results in 1200 V
 power electronics devices at a cost of 10 cents per Amp.

 3. Have Members of the Institute perform targeted applied research to provide evaluations of WBG
 reliability and system level performance advantages that will de-risk industry WBG product
 development cycles and decrease the time to WBG-enabled products, leading to 10
 PowerAmerica developed WBG PE technologies that are subsequently commercialized by
 industry within 5 years.

 4. Develop an educated workforce that will have the capability to innovate new WBG - enabled
 products to meet the future demands of WBG manufacturing, including at least 100 masters
 students and PhD students trained in WBG devices and Power Electronics. Within 5 years,
 prepare at least 500 workers with certifiable skills aligned with Industry Member needs for WBG
 power electronic careers through summer institutes, short courses and train the trainer activities.

 B. TASKS TO BE PERFORMED

BUDGET PERIOD 6

Budget Period 6 (BP6) is an additional budget period that will utilize program income accrued but not
expended during BP1 through BP5. In BP6, PowerAmerica will maximize benefit to its members by:
 • Conducting an Annual Meeting and a Summer Workshop
 • Maintaining silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) technology roadmaps updated
 through significant member participation at the Annual Meeting and Summer Workshop
 • Defining/selecting/managing Member-Initiated Projects at the direction of the MAC
 • Protecting intellectual property developed by the Member-Initiated Projects
 • Offering tutorials in SiC and GaN devices and applications that are held in conjunction with the
 Annual Meeting and Summer Workshop
 • Offering a detailed SiC and GaN Short Course annually
 • Participating in conferences with WBG content to promote U.S. based manufacturing of
 SiC/GaN technology and PowerAmerica’s members
 • Participating in IEEE and other roadmap activities and committees.

 In addition, PowerAmerica staff will continue to seek funding from external sources to contribute to
 sustainability and supplement member dues, especially to expand the number and scope of Member
 Initiated Projects.

 BP6

The objective of this project is to effectively manage and assess the performance of PowerAmerica: a

The PowerAmerica Institute is a consortium established under a Cooperative Agreement with the

form of the By-Laws and Operational Plan documents. These documents shall define the roles and

update the Organizational Structure documents as necessary to best achieve its technical and operational

Summary: Institute management shall develop and refine a strategic plan and provide updates to the

Task BP6-1.4: Device/Module Bank

Device/Module Summary: The purpose of the PowerAmerica Device/Module Bank is to create and
maintain a facility where advanced engineering samples of wide bandgap power devices and modules
can be readily obtained to accelerate the research and development of power electronic applications.
This facility shall also serve as a repository of information about WBG devices, data and datasheets for
 741

 BP6
the devices, and reference designs that use the devices.

The samples in the Device/Module Bank may originate from a variety of sources including through
member-initiated projects. (these samples become the property of PowerAmerica after the research
milestone is complete). Engineering samples may be purchased by PowerAmerica using the award’s
Program Income as it becomes known that the engineering samples will be needed for PowerAmerica
member-initiated projects.

In general, the samples in the Device/Module Bank are made available in the following ways:
1) PowerAmerica member initiated projects may use the samples for the completion of project work; 2)
PowerAmerica Members may purchase the samples for non-PowerAmerica purposes, thus gaining
timely access to advanced engineering samples of WBG devices that is not otherwise available to
nonmembers. 3) Unclaimed items from Device/Module Bank can be made available for sale to
nonmembers to recoup initial purchase and investment expenses.

Subtask 1.4.1 PowerAmerica will submit periodic reports on the Device/Module Bank inventory,
transactions and activities as part of the MAC and DOE quarterly reporting.

Subtask 1.4.2 Provide information to the Technology Roadmap task as needed to represent the current
and future availability of engineering samples.

Task BP6-1.6 Member Initiated Projects

Member Initiated Projects Summary: Member Initiated Projects in BP6 will be funded by program
income (including member dues and other member contributions) that was accrued during BP1 through
BP5. The projects shall address precompetitive problems of common interest to the industry and will be
selected by a membership voting process as outlined in PowerAmerica’s By-Laws. These projects will
be targeted to stimulate innovation and include device design and fabrication, packaging and modules,
reliability and ruggedness testing and gate drives, circuit simulations and design, and WBG power
electronic circuit integration for applications in the roadmap including automotive and rail traction, on
board chargers, power supplies, inverters/converters/rectifiers, portable power, aircraft and aerospace
electrification, renewable electric energy including photovoltaic/wind/hydroelectric, power grid
technologies, flexible alternative current transmission systems, high voltage DC systems, microgrids,
electric and hybrid vehicle power electronics, energy storage, wireless charging, motor drives, UPS, and
data centers.

Subtask 1.6.9 The process to initiate new Member Initiated Projects is defined below.
The PowerAmerica Member Initiated Project (MIP) process for BP6 will be as follows:
 1. PowerAmerica will submit to the DOE Technology Manager (DOE TM) for review and approval
 the request for proposal (RFP) that includes proposed topics, budget ranges, selection criteria and
 the review process to be utilized. Specific topics must be consistent with the scope restrictions
 identified in the Member Initiated Projects Summary above.
 2. PowerAmerica will issue the RFP after approval is received from the DOE TM. The DOE TM
 may need to consult and coordinate with EERE Management before approval can be given.
 PowerAmerica and the DOE TM shall coordinate review of draft RFPs prior to MAC consideration
 with the aim of providing DOE approval coincident with MAC approval.
 3. PowerAmerica and the Member Advisory Committee will review submitted proposals per the
 approved RFP and develop selection recommendations for DOE TM review and concurrence.
 DOE TM review is to ensure the selected projects are consistent with and support the mission of
 742

 BP6
 the Institute.
 4. PowerAmerica will submit budgets and SOPO documents for the selected projects to DOE.
 5. DOE Project Team and Contracting Officer (CO) will review each proposed sub-recipient project
 package. After any questions and issues are resolved, the DOE CO will provide MIP project
 approvals by email. As long as the projects fall within the scope and budget restrictions identified
 below, an award modification is not required to start work.
 6. PowerAmerica will issue sub-recipient agreements to DOE-approved MIP recipients based on
 their submitted applications.

PowerAmerica will provide progress reports on all active projects as part of its routine quarterly reporting.

Project Scope and Budget Restrictions:
For MIP projects to be selected and performed in Budget Period 6, the type of project work will be limited to
one or more the following: modeling, simulations, data analytics, device design, module packaging, and
technical assistance or intellectual/ academic/analytical activities (or similar activities). All work must be
conducted within existing facilities of the sub-award recipients and follow established environmental and
safety protocols. Project budgets are limited to $250,000 of Program Income provided by PowerAmerica.
Participant cost share (if required) is not included in the $250,000 limit.
Milestone 1.6.9.1 Institute shall provide the Member Advisory Committee and DOE with quarterly updates
regarding the status of determining project topics, soliciting proposals, funding projects, and project results.
(30 days after each calendar quarter)

Task BP6-1.7 Membership, Industry Relations and Communication

Membership Relations: The Institute shall implement a membership development program, including
membership engagement, recruitment and retention. The two primary objectives are: (1) increase
membership and assist member companies in growing their businesses specific to wide bandgap
semiconductor production and the use of wide bandgap technology in various systems, and (2) solicit
member guidance on short and long-term PowerAmerica operations and services that might provide

Advisory Committee and shall include the institute providing: (1) information about trends,

of wide bandgap semiconductors in various power electronics systems, (4) access to university programs
with access to students as future employees and faculty expertise, (5) member participation in wide
bandgap technology roadmapping that guides industry’s technology and product development
initiatives, and (6) workforce development programs, including short courses to help power electronics
applications engineers better understand and use wide bandgap semiconductors so this technology can
be designed into more power electronics systems.

FOCUS AREA 3

BP6-3.23 Demonstration of Advanced Power Packaging Technology for Near Term
Commercialization (BP6 Round 3 MIP)

Abstract: To provide a low cost, highly reliable near-term power packaging solution that the power
electronics industry can grow with, a new epoxy insulated metal substrate (eIMS) is proposed that can be
processed by high volume PCB/OSAT houses. The eIMS uses a new ‘high temperature, highly thermally
conductive organic dielectric having characteristics of 40kV/mm breakdown, 10W/mK and operates at
Tg≥300ºC with a low modulus. Half-Bridge GaN HEMT modules are demonstrated in a 400V/6.6kW,
1MHz charger at ≥98% efficiency.

The 10-mo. Project fabricates the GaN HEMT module, constructs the demo charger, and provides testing
results and a report. Delivery is 15 each fully tested GaN HEMT half-bridge known good modules
(KGMs) to Transphorm and PREES, and a design and test report to PA with sufficient detail for PA
members to reproduce results. (Up to three of PREES 15 modules will be delivered to PA.) Team
members and roles are given in ‘Teaming Section’. Risks and mitigation are given in ‘Technical and
Other Risks’ section. Graphics, Engineering Parameters, Descriptive Information, etc. are in ‘Technical
Description’ Section.

Subtask 3.23.2: Fabrication of ‘Single GaN HEMT Per Switch’ Module
Refine design, fabricate and test GaN HEMT module in the PREES Fab Srv Ctr.

Milestone 3.23.2.2 Electrical continuity success with KGD. (Month 10)

Milestone 3.23.3.1 Verified virtual design through simulations to meet testing criteria (Month 5)
Milestone 3.23.3.2 Verified final test circuit with surrogate devices. (Month 10)

BP6-3.24 Embedded GaN Power Module for High Frequency 400V/>20A Operation with Double-
Sided Cooling and Integrated Gate-Drive Circuit (BP6 Round 3 MIP)

Abstract: To meet the low-power module challenge, this project develops a half-bridge GaN power
module with double-sided cooling, low parasitic inductance, on-package decoupling capacitors,
integrated gate driver, and integrated common-mode choke. The module is realized by embedding two
GaN dies in a printed circuit board (PCB) with heat dissipation paths to a ceramic substrate from both
sides of the devices to achieve double-sided cooling capability. PCB’s low- cost manufacturing and
flexible layered-design yields a low-parasitic and highly integrated module, while the use of ceramic
substrate results in insulated thermal pad with exceptional thermal performance. Thermomechanical
performance of the module will be evaluated to ensure the reliability of the module design. Upon
successful completion of the project, the packaged power module would have immediate application in
EV battery chargers and dc-dc converters with improved high-frequency performance and compact
design.

Task summary include thermal design, die attachment layers, and electrical parasitics. An overly thick
ceramic layer could worsen the thermal performance while a thin ceramic might lead to early failure.
Similarly, the number and size of the thermal vias should be selected to optimize the thermal performance.
Different die attachment techniques yield different thermal expansion coefficient (CTE) mismatch
between the PCB and GaN die, which impacts the thermal cycling reliability of the module. To mitigate
the risk, substantial thermal management experience of power modules for mobility applications within
NREL will be leveraged for the evaluation of the UTK module. Guidance on transient thermal analysis,
computational fluid dynamics, and optimization of junction-to-coolant thermal resistance as a function of
heat transfer coefficient will be provided to UTK as needed. NREL will provide best practices on
experimental thermal characterization flow loops to UTK for experimental validation of the cooling
design. As part of the reliability test, a non-destructive thermal cycling test with 100 cycles will be
conducted by NREL to check if any severe degradation of the power module occurs during the limited
thermal cycling. NREL can also conduct vibration modeling and experimental evaluations under 15G x-
y-z axes vibration and 50G shock. Sinusoidal vibration and mechanical shock experimental evaluations -
using two modules provided by UTK - could be performed on NREL’s single-axis electrodynamic shaker
following the test standards.

the layout, start the fabrication process, and assemble the half-bridge module.

BP6 3.25 SiC-based Module Building Block with Integrated Inductor and Gate Driver (BP6
Round 3 MIP)

Abstract:
This work proposes to integrate 1.2 kV SiC MOSFETs with drivers, decoupling capacitors, and PCB-
winding inductors to build a 7 – 10 kW integrated power module building block (IMBB). ). By
integrating and codesigning these components together into a single universal module, higher power
density, improved efficiency, lower EMI, and smaller thermal resistance can be achieved. The IMBB
can be flexibly arranged to form different power converter systems, such as dc–dc converters, and
single- and three-phase rectifiers/inverters. Advanced packaging design will be used to minimize the
parasitic inductance inside the power and driving loops, enabling operating switching frequencies of 600
kHz – 1 MHz. With interleaving control, the equivalent switching frequency at the input terminal will be
1 – 2 MHz. This high switching frequency will enable the magnetics to be reduced, thereby increasing
the power density. State-of-the-art heat spreading materials and cooling techniques will be used to
effectively dissipate the heat from the SiC MOSFETs.

The proposed IMBB consists of a 1.2 kV SiC MOSFET-based full-bridge, gate drivers, decoupling
capacitors, and PCB-winding inductors. The IMBB will be realized using PCB as the base substrate,
which will interconnect the SiC MOSFETs, gate driver circuitry, decoupling capacitors, and inductor;
serve as the inductor winding; and dissipate heat from the SiC MOSFETs. FR4 and ceramic PCBs will
be evaluated. The SiC MOSFET bare die will be mounted onto the PCB to minimize the parasitic
inductance of the power and driving loops. Interleaving control will be used to achieve an equivalent
switching frequency at the input terminal of 1.2 – 2 MHz, which will enable the magnetics to be
reduced, thereby increasing the power density. To address the thermal and reliability challenges, ceramic
PCB inlays, TPG, and ceramic PCB (LTCC and HTCC) will be evaluated for achieving low CTE and
high heat dissipation. To mitigate the EMI, additional integrated inductors are included in the IMBB.

Subtask 3.25.2: Final Design and Simulation of the SiC Integrated Module Building Block
The heat spreader material and cooling method will be selected based on thermal FEA, and the design of
the PCB-winding inductor will be completed. The EMI of the IMBB will be analyzed using calculation
and simulation, and methods for suppression will be implemented into the design. The design of the
SiC-based IMBB will be finalized.

Milestone 3.25.2.1 Final design and simulation of the 7 – 10 kW, 600 kHz – 1 MHz integrated module
building block. (Month 6)

Subtask 3.25.3: Fabrication of the SiC Integrated Module Building Block
The IMBB will be fabricated by Virginia Tech. The prototype will include the 1.2 kV SiC MOSFET full
bridge, gate driver circuitry, PCB-winding inductor, decoupling capacitors, and thermal management.
Static electrical characterization will be performed on the prototyped IMBB to ensure electrical
functionality. The IMBB will be rated at >600 V and >20 A.

Milestone 3.25.3.1 Prototype and static electrical characterization of the integrated module building
block with >600 V and >20 A. (Month 9)

Subtask 3.25.4: Characterization and Demonstration of the Integrated Module Building Block
Thermal characterization will be performed on the prototyped IMBB to ensure sufficient heat
dissipation. Switching tests will be performed at the full power (7 – 10 kW), and switching frequency
range of 600 kHz – 1 MHz. The demonstration criterion for the IMBB prototype include verification of

BP6-3.26 Silicon Carbide Power Modules for Medium Voltage Applications (BP6 Round 3 MIP)

Abstract: The University of Arkansas (UA) working with NREL and Microchip propose a 1.7kV / 1600
A module architecture to address the PowerAmerica Module Challenge. This double-sided cooled,
switching leg configuration will consist of commercial SiC MOSFETs from Microchip along with their
commercially available digital gate driver to drive the MOSFETs. Additionally, buffer chips, decoupling
capacitors and gate-loop resistors will be included to mitigate loop inductances and gate oscillation
tendencies. An electrothermal co-design approach will be pursued ensuring full attention is given to
thermal management and reliability modeling to increase the lifetime of the modules. Cost and
manufacturing considerations will be taken into account from the beginning of the project to ensure
maximal technology transfer possibilities. The objectives are to design and fabricate up to three modules
for subsequent test and evaluation. The expected outcomes are the test results and lifetime predictions
from the project activity, along with recommendations for further development toward a commercial
module.

for this project can be summarized as follows. We intend to complete the design of the module concept
in the first 60 days and report that to the sponsor review team. The work will then progress to addressing
any design issues that emerge from the reviews and then orders for material will be placed. The team
will focus on any submodule assemblies that are felt necessary to either calibrate lifetime models,

BP6-3.27 Medium Voltage Solid State & Hybrid Breaker Architectures Using SiC JFETs (SUNY
Albany)

Abstract: In this project a detailed analysis of the application of SiC JFETs in medium voltage solid
state and hybrid circuit breakers will be analyzed. Modular hybrid and solid-state breaker topologies will
be studied for both AC and DC sub-stations using SiC JFETs of voltage rating 1.2kV or 1.7kV module
designs and stacking options will be analyzed. This will be followed by scaling the module rating up to
utilize fewer modules of device rating up to 6.5kV. A trade-off analysis will be done between single
6.5kV device implementation vs. series connection of 1.2 or 1.7kV devices, where efficiency, gate drive
complexity, controllability and cost. The project will be concluded with an economic viability analysis
of the proposed solutions and definition of device and gate drive design requirements to implement these
concepts.

BP6-3.28 Optimal HV SiC Device Characteristics for D-FACTS Rated 5 kV to 25 kV (EPRI)

Project Summary:
An important segment of electric utilities committed to de-carbonization of their generation fleets by
setting aggressive goals with deadlines starting in 2030. Hence, distributed energy resources (DERs), often
no-dispatchable and having fast power ramps, will become more prevalent in distribution systems. FERC
orders 841 and 2222 should lead to greater use of power electronics to control power flow in distribution
and transmission systems because of fast-response times required to maintain system stability and
resiliency. Equipment based on power electronics are broadly called distribution flexible alternating
current transmission systems (D-FACTS).
Concurrently, manufacturers of power semiconductor devices based on silicon carbide (SiC) have been
developing high-voltage (HV) SiC MOSFETs within the 1.7-kV to 10-kV range. SiC MOSFETs rated 1.7
kV are already commercialized, 3.3-kV devices should be commercialized within the next 12 months from
different manufacturers (e.g., Microchip, Wolfspeed) with 6.5-kV and 10-kV devices available in the form
of engineering samples. It is well known that SiC MOSFETs have technical advantages of silicon IGBTs
(e.g., lower losses, smaller footprints).
Consequently, the main goal of this proposal is to define the optimal static and dynamic characteristics of
HV SiC MOSFETs for selected D-FACTS applications which are representative of equipment that would
be required within the next 3 years and beyond. The results of this research should enable SiC MOSFET
manufacturers to develop roadmaps considering the current and voltage ratings of selected representative
applications.
Subtask 3.28.1: Characterizing selected D-FACTS applications for 5-, 15-, 25-kV distribution
systems
Subtask summary: The team has selected the STATCOM and energy storage, or a combination of these
two as representative applications that will be needed in future distribution systems experiencing greater
DER penetrations within the time targets mentioned above. UA and NCSU principal investigators will
work with EPRI to conduct a survey among member utilities to gather power and voltage ratings of these
two applications as well as any other equipment based on power electronics that may have a higher priority
within a particular utility. Technical requirements for the selected D-FACTS applications will be
determined based on the survey. For example, initial power ratings may be 1 MVA, 2 MVA, 5 MVA and
10 MVA.
Cascaded converters can achieve the desired grid voltage by connecting cells in series as shown in Fig.1.
The cascaded half-bridge (CHB) topology is selected as an interface between a medium-voltage (MV)
grid and the battery pack for energy storage applications. Galvanic isolation may be required between the
dc/dc and dc/ac stages; therefore, dual active bridge converter can be utilized as shown in Fig.1. In order
to cascade cells in series two options are available based on the voltage blocking capability of available
semiconductor devices; either fewer cells can be utilized with higher voltage blocking capability, or higher
number of cells can be utilized with lower voltage blocking capability.

Milestone 3.28.1.1: Report outlining the results of the D-FACTS survey. Technical specifications of the
selected D-FACTS applications will drive the work in subsequent subtasks. (Month 2)
Subtask 3.28.2: Cataloging the main characteristics of existing HV Si and SiC devices for the
selected D-FACT applications
Subtask summary: Silicon (Si) 3.3-kV IGBT modules are widely used in traction systems for electric trains
and HVDC voltage-source terminals with current ratings up to 2.4 kA. This maximum current drops to
1.8 kA for 4.5-kV IGBTs and 750 A for 6.5-kV IGBTs. Most HV SiC devices are not commercially
available (with the exception of 1.7-kV SiC MOSFETs with modules rated up to 378 A). The team will
catalog HV Si and SiC devices current available (either commercialized or engineering samples) for the
selected D-FACTS applications to determine their maximum switching frequencies resulting from a loss
analysis. Tables I and II illustrate some Si and SiC modules from a range of 1.7kV to 10kV. It can be
noted that the current rating of Si IGBT modules is much higher than those of SiC MOSFETs. For
example, five 1.7-kV SiC MOSFET modules would be connected in parallel to match the current rating
of a 1.7-kV Si IGBT module. However, the switching losses of this single Si-IGBT module would be 29
times higher than those of the paralleled SiC MOSFET modules. Therefore, SiC-MOSFET would have
the capability of operating at higher frequency compared with the Si-IGBT. Higher operating frequencies
should translate into higher power densities.
Milestone 3.28.2.1: A report comparing the different static and dynamic characteristics of existing HV Si
and SiC devices for the selected D-FACTS applications. (Month 2)

Subtask 3.28.3: Matching the HV SiC devices to the selected D-FACTS applications
Subtask summary: There are two options for connecting CHB directly to MV distribution systems:
cascading (i) lower number of cells using HV modules, or (ii) higher number of cells using modules with
lower blocking voltages. These solutions will be evaluated by considering suitable HV Si-IGBT and SiC-
MOSFET power modules to design the selected D-FACTS applications based on the CHB topology for
5-kV to 25-kV distribution systems. In general, interfacing D-FACTS to distribution systems via
multilevel converters involve evaluating several tradeoffs. For example, the output filter size is inversely
proportional to the effective switching frequency that is higher for lower-voltage devices capable of
switching faster but system becomes more complex.
