The team will determine the best voltage ratings of power modules for the 5-, 13.8- and 25-kV distribution
systems using the existing HV SiC MOSFETs. Figures of merit to consider are switching frequency,
efficiency, output filter size, power density, and system complexity. As the blocking voltage of a module
increases, the required number of cells reduces. Larger conduction power losses occur for higher numbers
of cells while higher switching power losses incurred for low number of cells. However, current ratings
of the modules are important. For example, a design considering 10-kV/90-A SiC-MOSFET modules
leads to a 5-level CHB with the same number of modules (36 modules) that a 13-level CHB due to the
limited current capability of 10-kV SiC modules. So, a system with higher number of cells and higher
number of modules will increase its complexity that may lead to increased rate of failure which can result
in unbalanced system voltage levels. On the plus side, quality of the output sinusoidal waveform improves
when a system has a higher number of cells, and hence, filter requirements become significantly smaller.
Preliminary initial designs of a three-phase 13.8-kV, 5-MVA, wye-connected grid-connected battery
energy storage system (G-BESS) using SiC MOSFET power modules were done as follows: Utilizing
CAS300M17BM2 1.7-kV/325-A modules led to a 25-level CHB with 3x12 cells where each power stage
(i.e., a H bridge) in the primary side includes 2 (half-bridge) power modules operating at a dc-bus voltage
of 1.2 kV. If 3.3-kV/500-A modules [18] are selected, a 13-level CHB with 3x6 cells where each primary
stage consists of 2 power modules operating at a dc-bus voltage of 2.4 kV. Employing 6.5kV/325A SiC-
 741

 BP6
MOSFET modules characterized in [3] form a 7-level CHB with 3x3 cells where each cell includes 2
power modules operating at a dc-bus voltage of 4.5 kV. Using the 10-kV/90-A SiC-MOSFET modules
characterized in [4] forms a 5-level CHB with 2x3 cells where each primary stage includes 6 power
modules and the dc-bus voltage is 7 kV. The secondary side of the DAB interfacing the battery pack
includes 1.2kV/450A modules from CREE operating at 600 V (or 800 V) to match battery packs voltage.
So, the transformer turns ratio will be 0.6/1.2 kV, 0.6/2.4 kV, 0.6/4.5 kV, 0.6/7 kV according to the dc-
bus voltage of the primary side.
Similar simplified analysis can be done for higher powers. The required number of cells for achieving a
particular grid voltage using 1.7-, 3.3-, 6.5- and 10-kV power modules would be the same but parallel
connection of modules would be required due to the limited current capabilities of available modules. As
an example, realizing a 10-MVA, 13.8-kV CHB interface with 1.7-, 3.3-, 6.5- and 10-kV modules results
in 3x12x4 modules (with 2 in parallel per leg of the H bridge), 3x6x4 modules (with 2 in parallel per leg),
3x3x4 modules (with 2 in parallel per leg) and 3x2x12 modules (with 6 in parallel per leg), respectively.
The gate driving complexity increases with the increase in the number of modules. The issue of
unbalanced transient current with respect to common source introduces mismatch of stray inductance.
Milestone 3.28.3.1: A report illustrating the various tradeoffs when using available HV SiC MOSFETs
rated 1.7-kV, 3.3-kV, 6.5-kV and 10-kV in the selected DFACTS applications for 5-, 13.8-, 25-kV
distribution systems. The tradeoffs are reflected in switching frequency, output filter size, power density,
system complexity, and efficiency. (Month 4)

Subtask 3.28.4: Defining the desired characteristics of HV SiC devices for the selected D-FACTS
applications
Subtask summary: The main objective is determining the gap between the characteristics of the currently-
developed HV SiC MOSFET modules and the characteristics needed for the selected D-FACTS
applications from a system perspective. The examples illustrated in subtask 3 shows that several power
modules must be connected in parallel for high power ratings of the considered applications. Reducing
the number of paralleled modules require higher current ratings, particularly for higher voltage SiC
MOSFET modules. This can be accomplished by paralleling a larger number of bare dies within the
module. However, several technical issues must be taken into account. For example, parallel transient
current imbalances with common source stray inductance mismatch can become more severe and
experienced on high- and low-side devices. So, there is a practical limit for paralleling bare dies and
beyond it may be easier to connect modules in parallel [19]. Another issue is that larger modules are more
susceptible to warping. The research team will explore this practical limit by interacting with module
manufacturers that are members of Power America Institute.
Milestone 3.28.4.1: A report defining the optimal characteristics of HV SiC MOSFETs for the selected
D-FACTS applications which are representative of equipment to have greater penetration in distributions
systems within the next 3 years and beyond. (Month 6)

BP6-3.29 Increasing Channel Mobility, Reducing Threshold Instability,and Improving Robustness
of 650 V SiC Power MOSFETs (Sonrisa)

We will evaluate recently-reported processes to reduce interface state density and increase inversion
layer mobility at the SiO2 / 4H-SiC MOS interface, and determine their suitability for use in commercial
power MOSFETs. This will include seven different oxide formation and anneal combinations on two
different oxide thicknesses, for a total of 14 different oxide interface processes. Measurements will
include Dit(E), oxide leakage, oxide breakdown field, charge-to-breakdown QBD, threshold stability
under NBTI and PBTI, and inversion layer mobility as a function of gate voltage from room temperature
to 175°C. Deliverables include all fabrication parameters, along with measured data on all MOS
capacitors and MOSFETs. The project will be coordinated by Prof. James Cooper, and all experimental
work will be conducted in the Birck Nanotechnology Center at Purdue University under the supervision
of Prof. Dallas Morisette. Dr. John Ransom, Technology Director of the SiC foundry at X-FAB Texas
will provide industrial oversight.

Milestone 3.29.1: Pre-oxide H2 etch and oxide formation on 14 MOS capacitor and MOSFET samples
complete. Due date: End of month 4.
Milestone 3.29.2: Post-oxide anneals on all MOS capacitor and MOSFET samples complete.
Due date: End of month 5.
Milestone 3.29.3: Final processing on all MOS capacitor and MOSFET samples complete.
Due date: Halfway through month 8.

Milestone 3.29.4: Characterization of all MOS capacitor and MOSFET complete.
Due date: End of month 12.

Deliverables include all fabrication parameters and electrical measurement data on all samples.
Counting both thin-oxide and standard-oxide samples, we will characterize 14 different thickness/oxide
formation/post-ox-anneal combinations. MOS capacitor data will include Dit(E), leakage current,
breakdown field, and QBD. MOSFET data will include threshold voltage at room and elevated
temperatures, threshold voltage stability under NBTI and PBTI, and mobility as a function of gate
voltage for all processing combinations.

Deliverables: Reports detailing fabrication parameters for each of the seven processes, along with

number of samples to PowerAmerica members at no cost. If a member requires a large number of

BP6-3.31 Demonstration of 100 kW SiC Inverter with Soft-Switching dv/dt Filter and Ultra High
Efficiency for Motor Drives (NCSU Yu)

Task Summary
This 12-month project will focus on designing, fabricating and prototyping of a 100 kW SiC inverter
with soft-switching dv/dt filter and ultra-high efficiency for motor drive. The project is expected to be
demonstrated in the switching frequency range of 5 kHz to 30 kHz. The measurements in the subtasks
are planned at a frequency of 18 kHz, which is much higher than the most common frequency of 5-10
kHz in the motor drives. NC State University will develop the soft-switching filter and SiC inverter
hardware and control method. Microchip Technology will provide SiC device selections and advice on
SiC device application and guidelines in a soft-switching dv/dt filter. NC State has all the equipment
needed for this project, including two fiber-optical voltage probes, high bandwidth oscilloscope, high
power supply and high-power loads. There are three major planned accomplishments for the project:
  Validate that the proposed design provides clear technical advantages of higher efficiency
 and reduced size/weight, and system-level benefits over the state-of-art dv/dt solutions in SiC
 inverters for motor drives.
  Conduct electric-thermal-mechanical co-design using cost-effective SiC MOSFETs, coreless
 inductor and ceramic capacitors for the soft-switching dv/dt filter. The high performance
 soft-switching dv/dt filter will be designed, fabricated and validated using a buck converter
 with soft-switching operation and targeted 6 kV/µs voltage slope.
  Develop practical implementation to meet all requirements of the targeted efficiency and
 targeted dv/dt for fully functional three-phase SiC inverter hardware rated at 100 kW output
 power, 99.2% system efficiency, and targeted 6 kV/µs voltage slope.

Task Description

Subtask 3.31.1: Technical Analysis of SiC Inverter with dv/dt Control (Month 1 - 3)
Three types of dv/dt control methods with active gate driving, passive dv/dt filter, and soft-switching
dv/dt filter will be systematically analyzed and fairly compared according to the quantified metrics
including total loss, overall size and weight, and total cost. The voltage slope dv/dt parameter will be
carefully evaluated. This task will document strengths and weaknesses of three dv/dt control methods of
SiC inverter for motor drive.
Milestone 3.31.1.1 (Month 3): Delivery of the analysis results of the SiC inverter with dv/dt control
methods.
Subtask 3.31.2: Development of Soft-Switching dv/dt Filter (Month 4 - 6)
The simulation platform for soft-switching dv/dt filter will be developed and used to evaluate soft-
switching dv/dt filter performance. The SiC devices used for dv/dt filter will be selected and evaluated.
A coreless inductor for dv/dt filter will be designed, fabricated and tested. The capacitors for dv/dt filter
will be selected and tested. The control method of the soft-switching dv/dt filter will be developed. A
buck converter will be used to validate the developed soft-switching dv/dt filter with the targeted voltage
slope.
Milestone 3.31.2.1 (Month 6): Completed fabrication and validation of soft-switching dv/dt filter with
targeted 6 kV/µs voltage slope.
Subtask 3.31.3: Demonstration of SiC Inverter with Soft-Switching dv/dt Filter (Month 7 - 12)
The three-phase 100 kW SiC inverter will be co-designed with soft-switching dv/dt filter. The 3D virtual
prototyping will be developed with the detailed electrical parasitics and thermal impedances. The
switching loss and device temperature will be evaluated. The gate driver for SiC power devices will be
designed with protection and the expected fast speed. The PCB based power stage will be designed,
fabricated and assembled to interconnect all components, including SiC devices, heatsink, gate drivers,

 747

Milestone 3.31.3.1 (Month 9): Completed fabrication and integration of SiC inverter with soft-
switching dv/dt filter.
Milestone 3.31.3.2 (Month 12): Demonstration of SiC inverter system at full power with 99.2%
efficiency and targeted 6 kV/µs voltage slope.

BP6-3.32 Paralleling of GaN modules for high power applications (GEAS)

GE-NCSU-NREL Team proposes to develop a high current GaN module with voltage rating of 650V
and current rating>400A. The Team will design active gate driver and demonstate parallel operation of
3 or more modules with current sharing within 5C of each other. The design proposed is for 3 die per
switch location and the internal design of the module will be scalable to higher currents with the
addition of die. While we list the specific PI for each task/milestone, GE Aviation is ultimately
responsible for the project execution.

Abstract: Usage of Gallium Nitride (GaN) devices for high switching frequency and high-power dense
operations are well known. However, commercially available GaN devices are limited in their current
rating. The unavailability of the high current rated GaN modules is a hindrance in the use of GaN in high
power applications. This proposal addresses this issue by first designing a GaN full-bridge module with
three 650V/150A dies in parallel offering >400A capability, then developing the means to parallel three
such modules to achieve total current rating in excess of 1200A.

Subtask 3.32.1 Design of GaN Full Bridge module (PI – Dr. Yang)
In Q1 a power overlay-based GaN full-bridge module will be designed. The module will consist of three
each 650V/150A GaN die in parallel per switch location. The module will have space for placing gate
driver totem pole stages and decoupling capacitors inside the module.

Milestone 3.32.1.1 Complete design for GaN Full Bridge module (Month 3) (PI – Dr. Yang)

Subtask 3.32.2 Gate driver design and GaN module testing
(PI - Subhashish Bhattacharya (NCSU))
In Q2 a Gate driver including the totem pole stage will be designed. The totem pole stage will be placed
inside the module. The performance of the GaN module with the totem pole stage and gate driver will be
evaluated via double pulse testing at +25C and +100C baseplate temperatures.

Milestone 3.32.2.1 Complete design of Gate Driver and perform module testing (Month 6)
(PI - Subhashish Bhattacharya (NCSU))

Subtask 3.32.3 DC bus bar design and parallel module testing
(PI - Subhashish Bhattacharya (NCSU))
In Q3 a DC bus bar and external gate driver will be designed to connect three GaN modules parallel.
The GaN module designed in quarter-1 will be paralleled in this quarter. The performance of the GaN
module will also be evaluated at +25C and +100C baseplate temperatures with a multi-stage
thermoelectric module.

Milestone 3.32.3.1  Complete DC Busbar design and perform parallel testing and evaluation of
Module. (Month 9) (PI - Subhashish Bhattacharya (NCSU))

Subtask 3.32.4 Active gate driver design and parallel module testing at different
temperatures (PI - Subhashish Bhattacharya (NCSU))

In Q3/Q4 a CPLD based active gate driver will be designed for improving the current sharing of parallel
GaN modules. The performance of the gate driver will be evaluated at different case temperatures, in
double pulse tests, and in continuous testing. The parallel module performance will also be evaluated in
overloading conditions. The short-time overloading capability of the parallel module will also be
determined.

FOCUS AREA 5

A: EDUCATION AND WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM

Focus Area Summary
Wide-bandgap (WBG) based power electronics have many characteristics that are superior to silicon-
based power electronics. WBG-based power electronics are expected to capture a significant portion of
the total power electronics market. They will be smaller in size, lighter in weight, and more efficient.
Benefits range from U.S. growth in power electronics related jobs to higher quality of life stemming
from cleaner and more energy efficient systems in sectors such as renewable energy, transportation,
information technology (data centers), industrial manufacturing, and consumer electronics.

Insertion of WBG-based power electronics into product sectors and adoption of this technology requires,
among other things, a WBG educated workforce. To this end, PowerAmerica’s Education and
Workforce Development (EWD) program is intended to catalyze growth of WBG technology awareness
and train the workforce through, short courses for working professionals, internships, and general
dissemination of information about WBG-based power electronics that will stimulate interest and
accelerate adoption.

Maintain WBG power electronics-focused collaboration of University students with industry.

In BP6, PowerAmerica will continue to offer short courses, technical webinars, and tutorials to working
professionals and students to ensure that we have an informed workforce in specific topics related to
WBG power electronics.

B: TASKS TO BE PERFORMED

BP6-5.6 Student Projects, WBG Short Courses and Tutorials

PowerAmerica will offer student educational projects, short courses and tutorials on WBG power
electronics to educate working professionals on the use and application of these technologies thereby
accelerating their adoption.

Subtask 5.6.1: PowerAmerica will solicit nominations from professors of PowerAmerica member
universities for one of their undergraduate or master’s degree graduate students to work on an education
project aimed at advancing silicon carbide or gallium nitride technology and falling under the project
categories and the scope limitations described in “Task BP6-1.6 Member Initiated Projects”. The project
will be defined in an application submitted by the university professor and student and must first be
approved by PowerAmerica’s Member Advisory Committee and submitted to the DOE Technology
Manager for review before work begins. Project outcomes will be presented at either the PowerAmerica
Annual Meeting (typically in February) or Summer Workshop (typically in August). A University may
submit only one project application under this category per 12-month period with a project budget not to
exceed $10K.

Subtask 5.6.2: The Institute will offer WBG tutorials at each Annual Meeting and Summer Workshop,
and WBG power electronics short courses to educate working professionals on the use and application
of these technologies thereby accelerating their adoption. Based on the feedback received from
